messages.subject: Instability of a model. In alpha[n] ~ (mu, sigma). Avoiding direct calculation of "alpha"
parts:
Hello,

I have a model of this kind

y[n] = lognormal(mu_1,sigma_1) * 0.5 + lognormal(mu_2,sigma_2) * 0.1 + lognormal(mu_3,sigma_3) * 0.4

OR

y[n] ~ Density( lognormal(mu_1,sigma_1) * 0.5 + lognormal(mu_2,sigma_2) * 0.1 + lognormal(mu_3,sigma_3) * 0.4, error)

Can I calculate mus and sigmas without calculating the intermediate parameter coming from that distribution?

For example


y[n] ~ Density( theta_1[n] * 0.5 + Theta_2[n] * 0.1 + theta_3[n] * 0.4, error)

theta_1[n] ~ lognormal(mu_1,sigma_1);
...
...

Here my model
data {
    int<lower=1> G;
    int<lower=1> S; // number of cases
    int<lower=1> P; // number of cases
    vector[P] a[S]; // predictor (covariate)
    vector[S] y[G]; // outcome (variate)
    real ex_mean_mean;
    real ex_mean_sd;
}
transformed data{
    vector[P] log_a[S]; // predictor (covariate)
    for(s in 1:S) log_a[s] = log(a[s]);
}
parameters {
    vector<lower=0>[P] log_ex[S,G]; // unknown true value
    vector<lower=0.00001>[P] ex_sd[G]; // prior scale
    vector<lower=0>[P] ex_mean[G]; // prior location
}
model {

    for(g in 1:G){
        for(s in 1:S) {
            log_ex[s,g] ~ normal(ex_mean[g], ex_sd[g]); // prior
            y[g,s] ~ lognormal( log_sum_exp(log_a[s] + log_ex[s,g]), 0.22);
        }

        ex_mean[g] ~ normal(ex_mean_mean,ex_mean_sd);
       
//Link function between SDs and MEANs
        for(p in 1:P) ex_sd[g,p] ~ gamma(2.27, (2.27 / exp(0.217 - 0.178 * ex_mean[g,p])));
       
    }
   
}

I didn't understand what you were asking --- what is ex_mean and
ex_sd?

In my case the intermediate parameter is log_ex.

This parameter (3d matrix) has just one observation for each element. One estimate from one observation has no info to converge (i imagine). However I only care about grouping log_ex and finding their distribution with parameters ex_mean[g], ex_sd[g], I don't care about log_ex itself.

I'm afraid that the low speed and mis convergence are caused by trying to calculate log_ex (of which I don't care of) just to be able to infer its mean and sd

-------------------------

As a note: If I only infer the mean ex_mean of each component of the mix, the model works beautifully

y[g,s] ~ lognormal( log_sum_exp(log_a[s] + ex_mean[g]), sigma);      //this is a deconvolution of the mix

If I try to calculate the standard deviation as well
y[g,s] ~ lognormal( log_sum_exp(log_a[s] + log_ex[s,g]), 0.22);
log_ex[s,g] ~ normal(ex_mean[g], ex_sd[g]);
-------------------------
What intermediate parameter are you talking about?

log_ex which I don;t care about, but I didn't find any other way to calculate it's mean and sd. The problem is that log_ex is 1 to 1 with observations. While it's mean and sd come from many log_ex and thus is a more robust parameter.

Is that y[n] being set to a mixture as written or was the intent
to draw it from a mixture?

y[n] is a data I have (gene expression) and I know that is the result of a mixture for which component I know the proportions (a[s])

Thanks.

- Bob

by "calculating" when you say calculating a variable leads to
misconvergence. Do you mean adding a new variable to a model?
Adding new parameters can cause problems if they're not identified.

In general, there's no way to estimate the posterior mean and standard
deviation of a parameter without sampling. Sometimes you can do it analytically.
For example, you can integrate out the beta a beta-binomial to get the
beta-binomial distribution and integrate out the gamma of a gamma-poisson
to get a negative binomial. Is that what you're trying to do? You
say you don't care about log_ex, but then you are asking for its mean
and standard deviation.

- Bob

The summary for a Stan fit isn't a confidence interval,
it's a posterior interval.

If you have two parameters a and b, you can't provide
a Bayesian answer to "are they different" because unless
one's a function of the other one, the statement Pr[a = f(b) | data]
will be zero.

- Bob

All it does is add a term to the log density. Then the prior

ex_sd, not just a calculation based on whatever ex is, even if

So mu is a parameter 3-vector, sigma is a scalar, y[n] is a known scalar,
and the a[n, ] is a known simplex?

And you want to ask a question about the marginal posterior

p(mu | y, a)

such as do the mu[1], mu[2] and mu[3] components have the same
posterior distribution?

How do you want to measure difference? You can look at one-sided
event probabilities like

Pr[mu[1] > mu[2] | y, a]

Presumably if that's a very high value, you know they're different.

But I don't think that's the question you really want to ask.

Usually, what people do is compare whole models, like a simple model,
two-component mixture and three-component mixture. Just because
a three component mixture has very distinct mu[1], mu[2] and mu[3]
posteriors, it doesn't mean it's giving you any added value over a two-component
mixture. But you have to decide what it is you value---some
prediction, perhaps?

- Bob
